criteria.rationale: For a lender the defining risk is who holds default risk. The deck says the credit book is on StockSathi's own capital with an NBFC 'in discussion'; the form says credit comes 'through our NBFC partner' with StockSathi taking first loss, and then asks the fund for NBFC introductions. That is a deck/form contradiction on the defining fact. There is no days-past-due or loss data, and nothing on whether the structure complies with NBFC registration or the digital-lending rules. Under C004 the claimed (unsigned) NBFC partner earns no credit as risk management; the personal follow-up on late payments is the only sign of ownership.

evidence.text: Deck: credit pilot funded from own capital; NBFC partnership in discussion. Form: credit provided through 'our NBFC partner', StockSathi takes first loss; form also asks for NBFC introductions.
Not registered as an NBFC; legality of own-balance-sheet trade credit and of the disbursal/repayment flow is not addressed.
First-loss cover under RBI's DLG framework is capped at 5%; the form gives no DLG percentage or form.
Credit book INR 85,000 across 12 retailers after four months; 'no defaults so far'; late payments followed up personally. No DPD data.
CAC contradiction: deck INR 2,860 (October, one town) vs form 'under INR 2,000', which is the deck's own 12-month target. Retailer count 38 vs 42.

gates.detail: Possible overlap with SuperK, a tech-enabled franchised kirana/mini-supermarket chain in small towns. It is a pre-fund partner investment (all_in_capital_fund_investment=false), but it is still in the portfolio list. Same customer (small-town kirana owners) and an overlapping job (stock supply, and possibly working capital, to those stores). The intro came through a Fund I portfolio founder. Per C003 the fund prefers a false alarm: Kushal should check with SuperK before proceeding. The full list was also checked. Mannjal (credit for B2B marketplaces) and Rocketpay (P2P collections) are adjacent on the credit layer but serve different customers. B2B marketplaces Magma, Hectar, Nirmaan, FanTail and Viralme serve different categories. No other same-customer, same-job match.

The core ordering business, earning trade margin, does not need a regulatory permission. The credit leg is not NBFC-registered and its compliance is unclear, but a standard NBFC-partner route exists and the founders are pursuing it. That is a serious R1/R4 risk, not 'exists only if the rules change'. Re-check on the call: if credit cannot be offered compliantly, a large part of the plan has to be rebuilt.

The sector label is a stretch. The founders selected 'Consumer tech', but this is B2B kirana distribution with embedded trade credit, i.e. lending ops. That matches the thesis example of 'fintech that is really lending ops'. Flag only (Jai Kisan precedent).
This is a pre-seed first round: INR 2 Cr at INR 12 Cr post-money, angels only. It is within the fund's lead mandate (first rounds up to ~INR 6 Cr).

case_for: Real on-the-ground work: 60 owner interviews before launch, in-person field onboarding, and channel-level CAC disclosed with its caveats (R2).
Early repeat behaviour is strong for a B2B ordering app: 22 stores reorder, about weekly (R3).
Domain fit on paper (FMCG distribution plus payments engineering) for small-town distribution, and a first round the fund can lead (S3, S2).
case_against: The defining lender question is unresolved, and the deck and form answer it differently. Deck: own capital, NBFC 'in discussion'. Form: 'our NBFC partner', StockSathi takes first loss, while also asking for NBFC intros. This counts against candour (R1).
Two more headline numbers differ between deck and form: retailers 38 vs 42, CAC INR 2,860 vs 'under 2,000' (the latter is the 12-month target) (R1, R3).
There is no compliant credit structure yet (not an NBFC, flow undescribed under the Digital Lending Directions), and 40% of the raise goes into the book (R4, R5).
Crowded, well-funded category (Jumbotail, ONDC/Qwipo, B2B BNPL). Possible overlap with SuperK needs a conversation first (S4, G1).
call_questions: Is there a signed NBFC agreement today? If yes, which NBFC, what DLG percentage and in what form; if not, on whose balance sheet is the INR 85,000 book, and why did the form say 'our NBFC partner'?
Have you taken legal advice on lending from your own capital without NBFC registration? Who disburses, into whose account, and where do repayments land?
How many credit orders have paid late and by how many days, and what loss rate does your plan assume at 300 stores?
What is today's retailer count, and what was October CAC including field-agent salaries? Why does the form say under INR 2,000?
What is contribution per order after delivery cost and expected credit losses?
Your deck and form tell two different stories about who funds credit. Walk us through how that happened. (Pressure test on the weakest point: we are watching for ownership versus defensiveness.)
what_would_change_our_view: A signed, compliant credit structure with a clear statement of who holds default risk, plus three to six months of repayment data (days past due, losses) on a larger book, reconciled with consistent traction numbers.
